name: Essential oil mouthwash (Listerine)

lead: Essential oil mouthwash, best known as Listerine, combines thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate. People use it daily for fresher breath and cleaner teeth and gums. It has been sold since 1879 and was the first US over-the-counter mouthwash.

The oils are described as disrupting bacterial cell walls, inhibiting enzymes and penetrating plaque biofilm. Systematic reviews find it reduces plaque and gingivitis versus brushing alone, and a commentary on a 2011 review found it may match chlorhexidine for long-term gum control while chlorhexidine is stronger on plaque.

paras: It is a standard daily rinse after brushing and flossing, used in many breath and gum care routines. Original and alcohol-free versions are both sold.
Original versions contain roughly 22 to 27 percent ethanol, which can cause burning or dryness; alcohol-free versions exist. Wikipedia describes the alcohol and oral cancer link as inconclusive.

angle.text: Listerine-style rinses are used daily for fresher breath and cleaner teeth and gums, with antiseptic oils cutting plaque and gingivitis. Trials show a modest reduction, with chlorhexidine still stronger on plaque.

lead: Essential oil mouthwash is a rinse whose active ingredients are thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate, best known as Listerine. Listerine was developed in 1879 by St. Louis chemist Joseph Lawrence and named after surgeon Joseph Lister, and it became the first over-the-counter mouthwash in the US in 1914.[1]

The appearance payoff is fresher breath and cleaner-feeling teeth and gums, which matter for close-range impressions and for confidence when speaking and smiling. Halitosis is a common concern: Wikipedia reports prevalence estimates of 6 to 50 percent and that most genuine cases, roughly 85 to 90 percent, originate in the mouth, typically from anaerobic bacteria on the back of the tongue producing volatile sulfur compounds.[2] A review of halitosis describes essential oil (Listerine) rinses as reducing breath-odor scores in people with moderate malodor even without tongue brushing, with few data beyond six weeks.[3]

The research base is largely about plaque and gum inflammation, the things that shape how gums and teeth look and smell over time. A meta-analysis of 29 six-month trials found that adding an essential oil rinse to brushing was associated with a 16 percent greater reduction in gingivitis and a 27.7 percent greater reduction in plaque than mechanical cleaning alone, though all included trials were industry sponsored.[4] A 2011 systematic review compared essential oil rinses with chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and a commentary on it concluded the oil rinses may be equivalent for long-term gingival control while chlorhexidine performs better on plaque.[5][6]

Essential oil rinses are used in many looksmaxxing oral care routines for breath and gum care, usually alongside brushing, flossing and tongue cleaning. Public discussion of the product also includes its marketing history, its alcohol content and debates about rinse effects on the mouth's microbiome.[1][7][8]

paras: Essential oil rinses are used before social situations and as part of daily oral care to reduce odor-causing bacteria. A review of halitosis treatments lists essential oil, zinc chloride and cetylpyridinium-type rinses as agents that lowered breath scores, and describes tongue brushing and toothbrushing as part of the usual regimen.[3] Wikipedia lists mouthwashes with chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride as having tentative evidence for halitosis, notes essential oils can reduce it, and says mouthwash does not replace brushing and flossing.[8][2] A 1994 review of mouthrinses notes that rinses have been used for centuries for medicinal and cosmetic purposes and that research on the ingredients is comparatively recent.[9]

Reviews of antimicrobial mouthrinses name chlorhexidine gluconate and Listerine as the two agents shown to inhibit or reduce plaque accumulation and the severity of gingivitis, with chlorhexidine reported to reduce plaque by about 60 percent and gingivitis by 50 to 80 percent.[10] Healthier-looking gums and less plaque build-up contribute to how teeth look over time.

In practice, Wikipedia describes a typical use as swishing 20 to 50 ml for about half a minute and spitting, and notes that using mouthwash immediately after brushing can wash away toothpaste fluoride, so many guidelines suggest spitting rather than rinsing after brushing and using mouthrinse at a different time.[8]

Lawrence licensed the formula to Jordan Wheat Lambert in 1881; it was promoted to dentists in 1895 and became the first over-the-counter mouthwash in the US in 1914.[1] The company merged into Warner-Lambert in 1955, Pfizer acquired Warner-Lambert in 2000 and Johnson and Johnson bought Pfizer consumer healthcare in 2006.[1]

In the 1920s Gerard Lambert marketed it against 'chronic halitosis', and from 1921 to the mid-1970s it was also sold for colds and sore throats, claims the FTC ruled misleading in 1976.[1] Wikipedia's halitosis article credits physician Joseph William Howe with coining the term in 1874 and, citing Freakonomics, says Listerine's campaign made halitosis a social concern as the company's revenue rose from about 115,000 dollars to over 8 million dollars in seven years.[2] A 2006 editorial and historical review, Listerine's long shadow, discusses how the marketing helped popularize halitosis as a condition people sought to treat.[7]
Mouth rinses are far older than the brand: Wikipedia notes early records from China, Greece, Rome and Ayurvedic traditions, and says the US product range grew from 15 in 1970 to 113 in 2012.[8]

The original formula contains eucalyptol, thymol, methyl salicylate and menthol in an ethanol base of about 21.6 to 26.9 percent; Total Care versions add sodium fluoride.[1] A review states the essential oils kill microorganisms by disrupting cell walls and inhibiting enzymes, and discusses penetration of plaque biofilm.[11] A 2015 laboratory study tested individual Listerine components and mixtures against oral bacteria.[12]
Alcohol in rinses acts as a carrier for the oils and flavor; Wikipedia says it can dry the mouth, which may worsen bad breath, and that alcohol-free brands also serve religious groups who abstain.[8]

Wikipedia cites reductions of 22.2 percent in plaque and 28.2 percent in gingivitis after six months, only slightly above the vehicle without essential oils (20.8 and 27.7 percent).[1] A 2015 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Dental Association pooled 29 randomized, observer-masked, placebo-controlled trials of six months or longer and reported summary odds ratios of 5.0 for a healthy gingival site and 7.8 for a plaque-free site when an essential oil rinse was added to mechanical cleaning, with plaque and gingivitis reductions of 27.7 and 16.0 percent; the authors noted that all included trials were industry-sponsored.[4]

A 2004 six-month trial randomized 108 adults to Listerine Antiseptic, 0.12% chlorhexidine or a placebo rinse and found the essential oil and chlorhexidine rinses had comparable antiplaque and antigingivitis activity, with the authors noting that side effects of chlorhexidine may limit compliance.[13] A review concluded that essential oil rinse may be equivalent to chlorhexidine for long-term control of gingival inflammation, while chlorhexidine appears to perform better for plaque control.[6]

A 3-day plaque model compared essential oil rinses with and without alcohol, and a feasibility study tested an alcohol-free essential oil rinse in institutionalised elders.[14][15] A trial in intensive care patients tested an essential oil rinse for mouth malodour.[16] A 1990 paper compared mechanical devices with antimicrobial rinses in plaque and gingivitis reduction.[17]

Product labels advise against swallowing and the rinses are not intended for young children; Wikipedia notes alcohol-containing mouthwash can cause poisoning if ingested, a particular risk for young children.[1][8] Common minor effects of antiseptic mouthwashes include taste changes, tooth staining and dry mouth, and allergic reactions can occur.[8] Wikipedia lists staining as a feature of chlorhexidine and cetylpyridinium chloride rinses.[8]

On alcohol and cancer, a 2020 systematic review of eight studies with 43,499 participants found that one study reported a link between alcohol mouthwash and oral cancer, two found it only at high rinse frequency and three found none; the authors concluded that mouthwash cannot be guaranteed to be an independent risk factor but that risk increases alongside other carcinogenic factors.[18] A 2022 Evidence-Based Dentistry review of the same eight papers concluded that alcohol mouthwash alone, without other risk factors, did not raise oral cancer risk or salivary acetaldehyde, but that where other risk factors exist it may add to risk.[19] A 2009 study measured salivary acetaldehyde in four volunteers after rinsing with 13 products and found levels above endogenous baseline.[20] Wikipedia describes the evidence as inconclusive, and the alcohol-free Listerine Zero launched in 2009.[1]

Antibacterial mouthwash also affects mouth bacteria that convert dietary nitrate to nitrite. A 2015 randomized crossover trial in 15 treated hypertensive adults found that three days of antibacterial mouthwash reduced oral nitrate-to-nitrite conversion and was accompanied by a small rise in systolic blood pressure.[21] Wikipedia presents links between antiseptic rinses, the oral microbiome and cardiovascular risk as associations from limited evidence.[8]
A 2007 recall covered about 4 million bottles of Listerine Agent Cool Blue over potential contaminants.[1]

Human studies include plaque models, trials in ICU patients and elders, and a radiotherapy mucositis feasibility study of manuka and kanuka essential oils in 19 patients, which reported delayed mucositis onset.[22][14][16][15] A systematic review compares essential oils with chlorhexidine, and a six-month randomized trial found comparable outcomes for Listerine and chlorhexidine.[5][13]

A 2005 controlled trial examined Listerine Antiseptic's effect on viral contamination of saliva, and a 1985 controlled trial examined how rinsing changes the properties of developing plaque.[23][24] A 2024 randomized substudy of the PReGo trial examined the effect of daily Listerine Cool Mint use on the oropharyngeal microbiome.[25] The OMEGA trial in 530 men randomized to Listerine or a comparison mouthwash for 12 weeks and found oropharyngeal gonorrhoea in 7 percent of Listerine users and 4 percent of comparison users, with no significant difference in cumulative incidence.[26]

Listerine's 1920s advertising is a standard case study in how a product can define a social problem, and the 2006 editorial Listerine's long shadow uses it that way.[7][2] Wikipedia notes people sometimes drink mouthwash for intoxication, which is one reason alcohol-containing products carry ingestion warnings.[1]

Wikipedia says the American Dental Association states brushing and flossing are usually sufficient while approving many mouthwashes, and that Americans spend over one billion dollars a year on mouthwash, mints and similar products, many of which mask odor rather than address its cause.[8][2]

lore.intro: Essential oil mouthwash is discussed in oral-care and looks communities as a fast way to fresher breath and as an adjunct for plaque and gum care, alongside debate about its alcohol and its effect on mouth bacteria.[1][8]
